text: You have num courses courses, labeled zero to n minus one. You're given pairs a, b, meaning you must take b before a. Return true if you can finish all the courses, otherwise false.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a pair a, b means b is a prerequisite of a. I can finish everything as long as the prerequisites don't loop back on themselves. Is that right?

So the whole question reduces to one thing — is there a cycle in the dependency graph? No cycle means I can finish; a cycle means some courses wait on each other forever. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Right, it's a cycle check. Up to about two thousand courses and a few thousand pairs.

Got it, so one linear pass over the graph is plenty. Let me run through an example. Say four courses, with pairs one-zero, two-zero, three-one, three-two. Course zero unlocks one and two, and both unlock three. No loop, so I return true. But if I had zero-one and one-zero, that's a two-course loop, so false.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. Each course is a node, each pair is a directed edge. Can I finish all courses is exactly: is this directed graph acyclic? This problem reminds me of cycle detection in a directed graph, and there are two standard ways to do it. DFS with three states — flag a node while it's on the current recursion path; if I ever step back onto one, that's a cycle. Or Kahn's algorithm — peel off nodes that have no remaining prerequisites; if I can't peel them all, the leftover ones sit in a cycle. Both are O of V plus E. I'll code the DFS one, then show Kahn.

Here's the plan for the DFS version. One: build an edge from b to a. Two: keep a visit array — zero unvisited, one on the current path, two done. Three: run the cycle check from every course, and fail on the first cycle. One thing worth flagging — the check needs three states, not two. In a DAG a node can be reached again through a different path; that's normal, not a cycle. Only re-entering a node that's still on the current recursion path is a real cycle. A plain visited flag would falsely flag the diamond's shared node. One more — I start the DFS from every course, not just course zero, because the graph may be disconnected and a cycle could hide where zero never reaches. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
DFS is good. Code it up.

Alright, let me code this up. I'll think out loud as I go. I build the graph with an edge from b to a, then call has cycle from every course and return false on the first cycle. Inside has cycle, state one means I walked back onto my own path, so that's a cycle; state two means the node is already finished and safe. Otherwise I mark it one, recurse into its neighbors, then mark it two. One thing worth flagging — setting visit of u to two before returning is not just tidy, it's what keeps this O of V plus E: a finished node is never explored again.

Let's dry-run the code on four courses, pairs one-zero, two-zero, three-one, three-two — so zero points to one and two, and both point to three. Expected: true. The row that matters is entering two and seeing three in state two — that call returns false right away instead of exploring three again. A two-state flag would misread that shared node as a cycle. Every course ends in state two, so the answer is true. Now the cycle case, zero-one and one-zero: I start at zero, enter one, and one's edge leads back to zero, still in state one. So the answer is false. Correct.
Good. You mentioned Kahn's algorithm — can you show that version?

Sure. Instead of recursion I track each node's in-degree — how many prerequisites it still has. I queue every node at in-degree zero, and each time I pop one I peel it by decrementing its neighbors; any neighbor that hits zero joins the queue. I count how many I peel. One thing worth flagging — the cycle check falls out for free. Nodes inside a cycle keep a positive in-degree forever, so they never enter the queue and never get counted. If done ends up below num courses, some courses are trapped in a cycle. Same O of V plus E, and no recursion-depth risk.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is O of V plus E for both — every node and edge is touched once. Space is O of V plus E for the adjacency list, plus O of V for the visit or in-degree array and the queue or recursion stack. Oh, one more thing — for very deep graphs the DFS recursion could overflow the stack, so in production I'd lean on Kahn's iterative version. And if I later needed an actual order of courses instead of just yes or no, both versions extend directly to produce a topological order.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You reduced the problem to cycle detection right away. You caught that the DFS cycle check needs three states — and showed exactly where a two-state flag would break on the shared node. And you flagged that you must run DFS from every course, not just node zero, so a disconnected cycle can't hide. Good work.
